Field notebook audio from the East Fork traverse, September fourteenth. This is Mara Ellis at the lower shale bench. The morning started under a flat gray sky, and the thermometer on the pack read six degrees Celsius at seven ten. The creek was low enough to cross at the usual gravel bar, but the north bank mud was still soft from last night's shower. I am forwarding the notebook scan to the county survey archive after we finish checking the station numbers. The paper original stays in the red map case until the team is back in town. The first station is EF twenty-one on the ridge side of the old cattle track. The brass tag is loose but still attached by one wire, and the painted arrow points northeast toward the basalt knob.

We walked from the road pullout at eight fifteen, carrying the hand level, two sample bags, and the short aluminum staff. The trail follows a cut made during the 1998 water line work, and the exposed rock there is dark gray, fine-grained basalt with small pale feldspar crystals. The west face has a rusty seam about twelve centimeters wide, and the seam gets thinner toward the creek. I measured its strike at 046 degrees and its dip at 63 degrees southeast using the compass clinometer. The reading shifted by two degrees when I stood beside the old fence staple, so I moved three meters uphill and repeated it. The second reading was 045 degrees and 62 degrees southeast. Jo checked the scale and wrote both readings in the margin because neither measurement should replace the other. The ridge surface has loose blocks of basalt and a patch of pale green lichen around the larger blocks.

The lower contact is not exposed at the trail itself, but a narrow wash below the basalt knob cuts through brown sandy silt and a layer of rounded pebbles. The pebbles are mostly quartz and chert, with a few dark volcanic fragments. The largest one I measured was seven centimeters across and had a thin white vein across one flat side. The silt is damp through the first four centimeters and dry below that depth. At the north end of the wash, we found a small spring seep beside a root ball. The water smelled faintly metallic, but there was no orange film on the stones and no visible foam. Jo said the seep might be draining from the rusty seam, but we did not trace a connection. The seep could also be coming from the shallow gravel lens above the silt. The water temperature was nine degrees Celsius, and the air at the same time was eight.

I marked the seep as EF twenty-two on the paper map and took a photograph with the ruler placed parallel to the channel. The scale in the first photograph is partly covered by my glove, so I took a second one with the ruler beside the wet edge rather than across it. Both images are on the camera card in folder East Fork Day One. The file names end in 184 and 185. The card display gives the time as ten forty-two, but Jo's watch was three minutes ahead, so the image time should not be treated as exact. We noted that discrepancy on the back of the map. The channel is about eleven centimeters wide where it leaves the root ball and disappears beneath a flat slab after roughly two meters. There is no safe footing on the slab because the surface is slick with algae and a narrow crack opens along its eastern edge.

Numbered section two: Sample handling. Number one: the first basalt chip came from the loose block beside the cattle track and not from the rusty seam. Its bag label is EF twenty-one A, and the mass is 312 grams. Number two: the seam chip came from the exposed west face at the point marked by a small orange flag. Its label is EF twenty-one B, and its mass is 184 grams. Number three: the silt pinch sample came from four centimeters below the damp surface at the north end of the wash. The label is EF twenty-two A, and the mass is 226 grams. Number four: we did not collect water because the clean vials were in the second pack, which stayed at the road pullout. The empty vials are still sealed, and their lot number is V seven thirty-one. Do not read that as a sample number. The three collected bags are inside a separate clear sleeve, and the labels are written in pencil as well as marker.

The field book page with the measurements is number thirty-eight, and the loose map insert is folded once along the creek line. On the page thirty-eight sketch, I drew the basalt contact as an observed edge only where it is visible and used a dotted line under the covered section. The dotted line does not mean that we confirmed the contact beneath the soil. The compass rose on the map insert is printed slightly off center, and the north arrow in my sketch comes from the handheld compass reading. The grid north and the compass north differ by about two degrees at this site. I wrote that note beside the scale bar so it is visible when the page is unfolded. The station coordinates were copied from the receiver after we moved away from the tall ridge face. The receiver showed an accuracy estimate of four meters at EF twenty-one and six meters at EF twenty-two.

After lunch, we followed the shallow wash east for about sixty meters and found two more bands of pebbles in the silt. The lower band is coarser and contains more chert, while the upper band has mostly quartz grains and fine sand. Jo estimated that the boundary between them is twenty-five centimeters below the top of the bank, but I did not measure it because the bank is undercut and a fresh piece fell when we stepped back. The fresh surface is damp and has roots crossing it from the grass above. There is no evidence in today's view that the bands continue beneath the basalt talus. The talus covers the slope for at least twelve meters, and the blocks are too unstable to climb safely. We photographed the exposed face from the path and made a note to compare the grain sizes with the west bank if that bank is accessible on the next visit.

If rain starts before the team returns to the road, the sample sleeve should stay inside the map case and not in the outside mesh pocket. The pocket zipper has a gap near the lower stop, and water got through it during the shower last night. If the road crossing rises above the marked gravel bar, we will use the upper footbridge and add its location to the map rather than attempt the ford at the lower bend. The forecast on the truck radio mentioned showers after four, but the ridge was clear when we packed up at one twenty. Neither condition had occurred by that time. We left the orange flag beside EF twenty-one B because it marks the seam point and collected the loose flag by the seep so it would not be mistaken for a station marker. The final page note says that the second basalt reading was made after moving uphill and that the first reading remains in the margin.

We returned to the pullout at two ten and counted three sample bags before putting the clear sleeve in the red map case. The camera card remained in the small padded case clipped inside my pack, and the handwritten page stayed dry beneath the map insert. The truck was parked with its front facing the road, and the rear wheel was on firm gravel rather than the soft shoulder. The clouds had broken over the ridge, but the shaded wash was still cool and damp from the morning. We did not revisit EF twenty-two or collect any additional material. The last entry in the notebook is the time we left the pullout and the note that the East Fork crossing was still below the gravel bar. The next person opening the book should be able to distinguish the observed contacts from the dotted inferred section and the photographed measurements from the approximate coordinates.

Mara uses the TideBoard browser extension to keep track of reading lists for three community projects. The extension sits in the browser toolbar, but she has chosen not to show its unread-item badge. She checks the lists during her morning planning session instead, usually on a laptop connected to the library’s guest network. Her preference is saved to her account, so the toolbar stays quiet when she switches between her home computer and the library laptop. The extension still opens normally from its icon, and the saved pages remain available in the list panel.

The preference is called “Show unread count on the toolbar.” Mara leaves it off because the number changes whenever a project coordinator adds a link, and she does not want a moving count to feel like a task she has to clear immediately. She still wants new items to be easy to find. In the list panel, unread links have a pale blue background, while links she has opened return to the regular white background. A small label beside each list name shows when that list was last updated. Those cues give her enough information without adding another number beside the toolbar icon.

Mara keeps separate lists for the neighborhood garden, the oral-history group, and the tenants’ association. Each list has its own color and a short description, and the colors appear in both the panel and the extension’s settings page. The garden list is green because it contains planting calendars and local soil reports. The oral-history list is purple and includes interview guides, consent-form examples, and audio equipment notes. The tenants’ association list is amber, with meeting agendas and explanations of maintenance rules. The color choice is only a visual label; it does not change the order of the links or the way the extension marks them as read.

1. Mara’s current preference arrangement has three parts:
   - The toolbar unread-count badge is off on all devices connected to her account.
   - Unread links remain highlighted inside the list panel.
   - The extension may send a weekly summary email, but Mara has left that separate setting off as well.

The distinction between the badge and the weekly email matters when Mara reviews the settings with a coordinator. Turning the badge on would not automatically enable email, and enabling email would not put a number on the toolbar. The settings page presents those controls separately, with a short description under each switch. Mara has asked the coordinator to look only at the badge preference during their next check-in. If the group later decides that a weekly email would help volunteers, they can discuss that option separately without changing the toolbar setting.

On Mondays, Mara opens the panel and sorts each list by the date it was added. She reviews the newest item first, marks a page as read only after she has checked its source, and sometimes leaves a link unread when she plans to discuss it at a meeting. The extension keeps the unread status attached to the saved link, even if she opens that same page in another browser tab. She does not use the panel’s automatic mark-all-as-read control because several items may still need review by another member of the project.

The extension also has a setting for opening saved links in a new tab. Mara has enabled it. That preference is useful when she is comparing an article with a meeting agenda, since the list panel stays open while the page loads separately. It is independent of the toolbar badge setting. Her usual process is to open the link, check the publication date and source, then return to the panel without closing the other project lists. If a page redirects to an unfamiliar site, she leaves it unread and adds a note to ask the group before sharing it.

Mara’s laptop sometimes disconnects from the library network while she is working. The extension keeps the list names and saved links visible, but it cannot refresh the update labels until the connection returns. She knows that a label showing yesterday’s date does not necessarily mean that no one added anything today; it may simply be waiting for a connection. The unread-count badge remains hidden during that time, as requested, and the panel’s existing highlights remain visible. Once the laptop reconnects, the extension refreshes the list information the next time Mara opens the panel.

The settings page records the date of the last change, which helps Mara remember whether she adjusted the badge preference herself or during a shared troubleshooting session. She has not changed it since the winter planning meeting. At that meeting, one volunteer said, “A quiet toolbar helps me notice the things I chose to check, rather than a number I have not dealt with.” Another volunteer preferred seeing a count, so the group agreed that each person could choose their own display. The extension’s shared lists do not impose one person’s badge preference on anyone else.

Mara plans to keep reviewing the three project lists every Monday and to leave the toolbar badge off for now. She will keep the unread highlights on, use the new-tab preference when comparing sources, and leave the separate weekly email setting disabled. If the volunteers later request a discussion about email summaries, that conversation can take place without assuming that Mara wants the badge enabled. Until then, she can find newly added material in the panel, check its source, and decide whether it is ready to share with the relevant group.

Last Thursday, I was at the north end of Briar Market before seven because our stall had a delivery of apples, pears, and jars of cider arriving from the orchard outside Millford. The market had moved the produce vans to the east gate while workers repaired the paving beside the old fountain, and our usual unloading space was blocked by orange barriers. I had sent the driver a map the night before, but the map still showed the old entrance, so I called Mara, who runs the stall with me, and asked her to stand by the new gate with the blue handcart.

We had ordered twelve wooden crates of apples, four crates of pears, and six boxes of cider, but the orchard message said one box might be held back if the jars had not finished cooling by dawn. That condition mattered because we had promised a small cafe the first two boxes by eight thirty, and I did not want to charge them for stock we could not hand over. Mara said the driver had confirmed all six boxes on Wednesday evening, but she would check the seal before she signed the delivery sheet. I said, “Yes, leave the cafe order separate until we see what arrives.”

The van did not arrive at six—no, sorry, six fifteen was the time the driver gave us in his last message—and he reached the gate at six twenty-two with his hazard lights on. He was called Joel, and he said the road from Millford was slow because a tractor had stopped near the river bridge. He apologized for not updating us sooner. I said that was fine, as long as we could unload before the first shoppers came through. He lowered the ramp, and we could see that the apple crates were stacked at the front, with the pears behind them and the cider boxes held upright near the cab.

Mara checked the labels while I counted the crates, and we both found the right quantities of apples and pears. One apple crate had a split slat, but the fruit inside looked sound. Joel offered to put that crate last on the handcart so it would not take the weight of another box. I agreed and wrote a note beside the crate number on the sheet. He had six cider boxes, too. The cardboard corners were damp, but the jar dividers were dry. When Mara asked whether we had enough paper sleeves for the cider display, I said, “Right, we do,” because I brought the spare bundle from the storeroom yesterday.

For the numbered section, give three checks:
1. Check the item count against the orchard note.
2. Check the jar dividers and labels before moving the cider.
3. Keep the split apple crate on the lower shelf and mark it for inspection at the stall.

We followed those checks in that order. The labels matched the orchard note, the dividers were dry, and none of the jars was cracked. Joel waited while I marked the split crate with a strip of green tape. Mara moved the cider boxes to the handcart without tilting them, and I kept the signed sheet on a clipboard so it would not get wet on the pavement.

When we reached the stall, the ground under the awning was still wet from overnight rain, so Mara put down the rubber mat before we unloaded the fruit. We set the pears on the left table and the apples on the right, with the cider in two rows behind them. I moved the crate with the split slat beneath the right table instead of putting it out for sale. Mara said, “Keep that crate aside until we have checked every apple.” I took that to mean we should not mix its fruit with the other crates, and we kept the green tape on the side facing the aisle.

The cafe owner, Leonie, arrived at eight twenty-five and asked whether the two boxes she had ordered were ready. I told her we had six boxes and that the jars and dividers had passed our check. She looked over the handwritten label on the first box and asked for one box of dry cider and one of the apple-pear blend. Those were both in stock, so Mara set them beside the till while I made a receipt. The owner asked if we could bring the boxes to her back door before nine if the rain stayed light. I said we could carry them over after the first rush, but if the rain became heavy, we would wait under the awning and call her rather than leave the boxes outside.

At eight forty, the market steward came by to check the space beside our stall. He told us to keep the handcart inside the painted white line because the bakery next door needed a clear route for its flour trolley. We moved it and left the aisle open. A customer then bought a bag of pears and asked whether the cider came from Millford or from the hills to the south. I showed her the small orchard label that named Millford, and she chose the apple-pear blend. She said she had tasted it at the autumn fair and wanted a jar for a neighbor. We wrapped it in one of the paper sleeves and put the lid upright so it would not press against the fruit.

Before nine, Mara and I counted the remaining cider boxes and found four sealed boxes still under the table. The cafe receipt and delivery note were clipped together in the till drawer. The split apple crate remained separate with its green tape, and Joel had taken the signed sheet back with him. The rain eased, but the pavement stayed slick, so we did not take the cafe boxes across the market until Leonie called to say her back entrance was clear. We kept the boxes beneath the awning and left the handcart within the marked line while the stall opened for the morning shoppers.

Leonie wartete schon am Schuppen und hatte die Anlage am Hauptschalter ausgeschaltet. Sie sagte: „Hier tropft es seit gestern Abend.“ Und ich antwortete: „Ja, dann schauen wir erst auf die Verbindung und nicht gleich auf die ganze Pumpe.“ Das „Ja“ war meine Zustimmung dazu, dass wir die Stelle gemeinsam prüfen und nicht bloß ein Geräusch beim Reden.

Am Verteiler haben wir zuerst den Filterdeckel angesehen. Der Deckel war außen trocken, aber unter dem Rand saß eine dünne Schicht Sand und kleine braune Blätter. Leonie sagte: „Gut, dass du das vorher gesagt hast, sonst hätte ich die Zeitschaltuhr schon auf den Nachmittag gestellt.“ Ich habe geantwortet: „Ja, der Wert ist noch zu niedrig, und wir müssen den zweiten Abschnitt ebenfalls ansehen.“

Für die Querleitung haben wir die Abdeckung am kleinen Schacht neben dem Pfirsichbaum angehoben. Darin standen ungefähr zwei Fingerbreit Wasser, und am Boden lag ein Stück weißer Kunststoff, das aus einer alten Klemme gebrochen war. Die Rohrwand war dort sichtbar, aber nicht nass. Wir haben das Wasser mit einem Becher ausgeschöpft und die Verbindung trocken gerieben. Während wir warteten, erzählte Leonie, dass der Schacht im letzten Sommer nach starkem Regen ebenfalls voll gewesen sei. Leonie schrieb neben den dritten Punkt, dass der Haupthahn bis zur weiteren Prüfung nicht ganz geöffnet werden soll. Wir haben außerdem die genaue Uhrzeit eingetragen. Es war 8 Uhr 35, und die Außentemperatur lag bei ungefähr 6 Grad.

Zum Schluss haben wir die Anlage kurz am Hauptschalter eingeschaltet und nur den Verteiler laufen lassen. Die Kupplung blieb trocken, aber am Pfahl zeigte das Messgerät weiterhin 1,6 bar. Darum haben wir die untere Reihe geschlossen gelassen und den nächsten Prüfschritt für Mittwoch angesetzt, nicht für Dienstag, wie ich zuerst gesagt hatte. Am Mittwoch will Leonie die Querleitung vom Schuppen bis zum Pfirsichbaum Abschnitt für Abschnitt öffnen und dabei den Druck an jeder Kupplung notieren. Wenn sich vorher noch einmal Wasser im Schacht sammelt, soll sie mir ein Foto schicken und den Haupthahn geschlossen lassen. Ich habe den Druckmesser wieder in den Koffer gelegt und die Karte mit den vier Punkten an der Schuppentür gelassen. the volunteer transport rota covers rides for people who cannot easily reach the clinic, the food hub, or the Wednesday advice desk. We have nine regular drivers and three people who can fill in when they are free. The rota is kept in a shared spreadsheet, but a printed copy is also in the blue folder at the community room. It is updated on Sunday evening for the week ahead. On Monday, Mira checks that the phone numbers and pickup notes are still readable, because small changes can get missed when people edit the sheet on their phones. The service does not promise a particular vehicle, only a lift with enough space for the passenger and any mobility equipment they have told us about.

The current arrangement began after the clinic changed its appointment times in March. Before that, most trips were grouped around the morning opening, and drivers could often do two journeys in one run. Appointments now start at different times, so the spreadsheet has separate rows for each pickup rather than one broad morning slot. A passenger's appointment time is written beside the pickup time, but not their medical reason for going. We keep that information off the rota. The clinic entrance is on Alder Street, while the drop-off point used by the advice desk is the side door on Mill Lane. New drivers have occasionally gone to the wrong entrance, so the location is written out in full in each relevant row.

There are two vehicles with wheelchair ramps, and both are owned by volunteers rather than the group. One driver has asked for at least a day's notice before a ramp trip, since the van also has family use. We mark that availability in the spreadsheet, but a mark is not a booking until the driver confirms by text. I think that distinction is usually understood, although it has caused a little confusion when someone has looked only at the printed copy. The rota lead, Sana, sends a confirmation message once a driver has accepted. If no one confirms by 6 p.m. the day before, the trip stays marked as unfilled and Sana calls the passenger to explain that the group is still looking.

For ordinary trips, passengers are asked to be ready ten minutes before the listed pickup time. That gives the driver a little room if the street is busy, and it avoids making another passenger wait on a shared run. We do not tell people to wait outside in bad weather; they can remain indoors and watch for the car. Drivers are asked to ring the doorbell once and wait up to five minutes, then call the number on the rota. If there is no answer, they should contact Sana before leaving. This has been useful when a passenger has been delayed inside the building, but the driver should not assume that is the reason for a missed response.

The group has agreed to use the north entrance at the clinic for passenger drop-offs, because the south entrance has a steep curb and little space to stop. On wet days, the paved section by the north entrance can collect water. If the water covers the painted crossing line, drivers should not stop at that entrance; they must call Sana and agree another safe place with the passenger. This condition matters because a recent note on the printed sheet still says “use the north door in all cases.” Sana has said, “That wording is too broad; the water rule applies even when the north entrance is normally the right one.” We have not yet replaced every old printed copy, so drivers are told to follow the current spreadsheet note if the two versions differ.

A volunteer can offer a whole morning or a single journey, and the sheet should show which one they mean. If a driver withdraws after accepting, they need to message Sana directly rather than only deleting their name. That gives her a chance to contact the passenger and find another driver. We have sometimes had people edit the same row at once, which is why changes to an accepted ride should be sent as a message as well as entered in the sheet.

2. The passenger details are limited to a name, pickup address, contact number, destination, appointment or arrival time, and practical notes such as a step-free entrance. The information is for arranging the lift and is not copied into the group chat. Drivers can see the rows assigned to them, while Sana can see the full week. After a trip is completed, the driver marks it done; Sana removes the passenger's details from the working sheet at the end of the month. A paper copy from an earlier week should be put in the locked office drawer for shredding, not left in the car or the community room.

3. When a passenger asks to bring someone with them, the driver needs to confirm there is a seat before the rota is changed. That second person is not automatically included just because they are named in a phone message. The same check applies to a folding wheelchair or a large walking frame if it was not mentioned when the ride was first arranged. The group can usually fit one companion in a standard car, but that depends on the vehicle and the equipment going with the passenger. Sana records the confirmed arrangement in the row so that the person taking the trip has the same information as the driver.

The food hub trip is generally the busiest one, particularly on the first Wednesday of the month, when several people collect larger parcels. The hub asks cars to use the marked lay-by behind the library and not block its delivery gate. Volunteers should not carry parcels into a passenger's home unless that person has asked and the driver is comfortable doing so. A passenger may need an extra minute to secure a bag or fold a trolley before getting into the car, and the pickup notes can mention this without giving a reason. I am perhaps slightly cautious about promising exact arrival times on that run, because traffic near the library varies, but the driver can send a short update if they expect to be more than fifteen minutes late.

There is also a monthly review at the community room, usually on the last Thursday, where Sana checks how many rides were completed, cancelled, or left without a driver. The figures are counted from the spreadsheet, not estimated from memory. Volunteers can raise practical problems there, including a confusing entrance note or a pickup time that repeatedly leaves too little room. Last month, one driver said, “I can manage the clinic, but I need the Mill Lane direction written before the name of the desk.” Sana changed the wording in the new rows to put the destination entrance first. The old rows are not all rewritten unless that trip is booked again, so the driver should check the week’s entry rather than assume every saved note has been updated.

The facilities analytics team moved its shared documents from the aging Northstar drive to the company’s new Cedar workspace over three weeks in April. The migration covered 684 files in 47 folders, including inspection schedules, vendor records, floor plans, maintenance notes, and the team’s monthly energy reports. The purpose was to give staff one searchable home for current material while keeping older records available for reference. No documents were deleted during the move, and the original Northstar drive stayed read-only until the team finished its checks.

The work was coordinated by Lena Ortiz, who maintained the migration tracker, and Dev Shah, who handled access settings and folder permissions. Each department named a reviewer to confirm that its files had arrived intact. The reviewers included Marco Bell from building operations, Priya Nair from procurement, and Jo Kim from sustainability. They met twice a week, but most questions were handled in a shared issue log so that decisions and follow-up tasks would remain visible to the whole group. Lena said, “We want people to find the right document without having to remember which person last touched it.”

Before copying began, the team compared the folder list against the archive inventory from the previous December. That comparison found 23 files with duplicate names, 11 folders with unclear owners, and four spreadsheets that depended on links to other Northstar files. The duplicate names were not automatically treated as duplicate content. Reviewers opened both versions, compared their dates and contents, and recorded which one should be treated as current. When they could not tell, they left both copies in a clearly labeled review folder rather than choosing on someone else’s behalf.

1. Migration sequence

The team moved the material in three batches. The first batch contained the shared templates and current operating procedures, because staff needed those files during the move. The second covered vendor and maintenance records. The final batch contained older reports and reference material. Dev copied each batch overnight, then ran a file-count and checksum comparison the next morning. A checksum is a calculated value used to help detect whether a file changed during transfer; it does not confirm that the contents are accurate or useful. Lena updated the tracker only after the reviewer for that folder had checked the file list and opened a sample of documents.

The team also tested links and permissions instead of relying only on the transfer report. Some spreadsheets opened correctly but still pointed to a source file on Northstar. Dev listed those links in the issue log and assigned their owners to update them in Cedar. A few floor plans were too large to preview in the browser, so Marco checked that they downloaded and opened in the team’s design software. Priya found that two purchasing forms were visible to the wrong group after an inherited permission carried over. Dev corrected those settings before the forms were announced as ready.

During the second week, the team learned that a set of inspection photos had been stored inside a folder labeled “Old site visits,” even though several photos documented current equipment. Jo asked the relevant building staff to identify the recent images, and they moved only the confirmed files into the current inspection folder. The older images remained in the archive with their original dates. Jo wrote, “A familiar filename is not enough to decide where a record belongs.” That distinction mattered later when reviewers checked the final counts: the team could explain why some files were retained in two locations without assuming that the copies were accidental.

The migration depended on one operational condition. If any department found a missing file or an unexpected permission during its review, that folder would stay on the tracker as unresolved, and the Northstar drive would remain read-only but available until the issue was investigated. If no such issue remained, Lena could mark the folder complete after its reviewer confirmed the count and access. This rule meant the team did not have to delay every folder while one department investigated a separate problem. It also meant that a folder could not be labeled complete just because its files appeared in Cedar.

2. Review and handoff

At the end of the third week, the tracker showed 47 folders copied, 42 accepted, and five still under review. Three of the five needed owners to confirm which of two similarly named files was current. One contained an old spreadsheet with a broken link, and one had a permission question from the finance liaison. The team kept all five marked unresolved rather than reporting the migration as finished. The reviewers checked the accepted folders against their inventories, and Lena saved a dated copy of the tracker in Cedar so the group could compare later changes with the handoff record.

Dev prepared a short access guide with instructions for finding the workspace, requesting access, and reporting a broken link. He included the name of the Cedar support channel and explained that staff should not email sensitive vendor documents to request help. We were expecting the ceramics delivery at the north entrance of the Harper Street Community Studio on Thursday the twelfth. The order was for the spring teaching sessions, and the invoice listed thirty-six pieces from Alder Kilnworks in Portland. The studio manager is Lena Morris, and I was helping her check the shipment because she had to teach a class at eleven. The carrier called at 7:45 and said the truck was running about twenty minutes late, so we moved the folding table away from the entrance and put the receiving clipboard on the shelf by the sink. The forecast said light rain before noon, but the loading area was covered by a metal awning, and there was room to back a small truck in without blocking the alley.

Lena had reserved the east workroom for the crates because it has a level floor and a wide door. The room is usually used for glaze mixing, but the materials had been moved into two locked cabinets the week before. We checked the door opening at thirty-nine inches and confirmed that the tallest crate should fit through sideways. The original delivery note said, “Arrive at nine”—no, sorry, “nine thirty,” and that was the time Lena had written on the class schedule. The studio has two hand trucks, but one has a loose strap, so we kept it in the closet and used the blue one with the rubber wheels. The supplier had wrapped each piece separately in paper and packed the bowls between layers of corrugated board.

The driver arrived at 9:28 in a white box truck with the company name printed on both doors. His name was Martin, and he asked whether we wanted the crates left at the curb or brought inside. Lena said, “Inside, please, but only to the east workroom,” because the front gallery was open for a small exhibit and we could not stack boxes near the display shelves. Martin checked the delivery number against the paperwork and said he had four crates, not three. The packing list did show four, and Lena counted them before anyone began unloading. One crate had a blue corner label marked “fragile,” and another had a strip of green tape around the lid. We took photographs of the labels before moving anything.

While Martin lowered the first crate, the left wheel of the hand truck caught on a shallow crack in the pavement. The crate tilted a little, but he steadied it before it touched the ground. He said there was no impact, and we did not hear anything shift inside. Lena replied, “Right, thanks for catching it,” and asked him to pause while she checked the lower edge. The wood looked intact, and the label was still fixed to the side. Martin then set the crate upright on the rubber mat, and we rolled it through the wide doorway. The other three came in without any trouble. One had a handwritten note saying, “Keep this side up,” and we kept that note facing the ceiling the whole time. The truck stayed in the alley for twenty minutes and did not block the neighboring bakery entrance.

1. The invoice lists twelve shallow bowls, twelve medium bowls, and twelve small pouring cups, for a total of thirty-six pieces.
2. The first crate held all twelve shallow bowls, wrapped in pairs, and the second held the twelve medium bowls in three cardboard dividers.
3. The third crate contained the twelve pouring cups and a small packet of replacement labels.
4. The final crate held packing material only, and the driver explained that it was a returnable crate that Alder Kilnworks would collect on its next route. Lena wrote that note on the delivery receipt before signing. The first three crates had intact seals, but the fourth crate had a broken paper seal already mentioned on the carrier sheet.

After the driver left, we set the crates along the north wall and checked the pieces against the packing list. There were no chips in the first two crates, but one pouring cup in the third had a hairline crack running from the rim about two centimeters down. We did not wash it or put it near the sink because the studio policy is to keep damaged pottery dry until the supplier responds. Lena took a close photograph with a ruler beside the crack and another photograph showing the cup in its original paper wrap. She placed both images in the delivery folder and wrote the time as 10:12. The rest of the cups looked clean, and the replacement labels were still sealed in their small plastic bag.

Lena called Alder Kilnworks at 10:20 and spoke with their dispatch coordinator, Nora Bell. Nora asked for the order number, the photographs, and the number printed beneath the cup. She said she would open a damage report, but did not say whether the cup would be replaced or credited. She also asked us to keep the broken cup and its wrapping until the report had been reviewed. Lena repeated that we would not discard either item, and Nora said she expected to send an update by Monday afternoon. That timing mattered because the first class using the new pieces was scheduled for Tuesday. If the replacement cup does not arrive before that class, Lena can borrow one plain cup from the neighboring pottery room, but only if its foot ring measures at least four centimeters.

We reviewed the receipt before Martin drove away and noticed that the printed count beside the returnable crate was written as one, but the box for “returned today” was left blank. Lena asked Martin whether he needed a signature in that box. He said no, because the empty crate was staying with us for his next route, and his office would mark it as pending return. She added his explanation beside the printed count and kept a copy of the signed page in the blue binder. Martin took a photograph of the four crates in the workroom and showed Lena the image before he left. He did not take the damaged cup because it had not yet been reported, and the supplier had asked us to hold it.

By eleven o’clock, we had finished the count and put the undamaged pieces on the lower shelf of the east workroom. The shallow bowls went on the left and the medium bowls went on the right, with a strip of cardboard between them so they would not touch. The cups stayed in their original wraps in a covered tray. Lena left the damaged cup in a separate carton on the upper shelf, with the photographs printed and tucked into the folder beside it. She wrote, “Do not use pending supplier review,” on a yellow note and dated it Thursday the twelfth. The note was meant for the afternoon instructor as well as the weekend volunteers.

The rain began just after noon, and the covered loading area kept the crates dry. The alley was clear when the bakery received its flour delivery later that afternoon. Lena sent the receipt and two photographs to Nora and copied the studio administrator on the email. She included the note about the broken seal on the empty returnable crate and asked whether the driver could collect it on Monday if he was already nearby. Nora had not confirmed that collection, and Lena did not mark it as arranged. The sealed replacement-label packet remained in the workroom drawer while the crack report stayed open in the delivery folder.

Die Rückmeldung soll an mich gehen, damit ich sie an die Gruppe weitergeben kann; ich bitte nicht darum, den Plan ohne Prüfung sofort zu veröffentlichen.
